## Working with Data

**WD-1: I can import data from a *variety* of formats (e.g., csv, xlsx, txt, etc.).**

-   `csv` Example 1

```{r}
#| label: wd-1-csv-1

#Lab 2 Question 1

surveys <- read_csv(here::here("Week 2","Lab 2", "surveys.csv"))

```

-   `csv` Example 2

```{r}
#| label: wd-1-csv-2

#Lab 3 Question 2

teacher_evals <- read_csv(here::here("Week 3","Lab 3", "teacher_evals.csv"))


```

-   `xlsx`

```{r}
#| label: wd-1-xlsx

#PA 4 Question 1

library(readxl)

military <- read_xlsx("gov_spending_per_capita.xlsx",
                      sheet = "Share of Govt. spending",
                      skip  = 7,
                      n_max = 190,
                      na = c(". .", "..", "xxx")
                      )

```

**WD-2: I can select necessary columns from a dataset.**

-   Example selecting specified columns

```{r}
#| label: wd-2-ex-1

#Lab 3 Question 5

teacher_evals_clean <- teacher_evals |>
  rename(sex = 'gender') |> 
  mutate(teacher_id = as.character(teacher_id)) |> 
  filter(no_participants > 10) |> 
  select(course_id, teacher_id, question_no, no_participants, resp_share, SET_score_avg,
         percent_failed_cur, academic_degree, seniority, sex)

```

-   Example removing specified columns

```{r}
#| label: wd-2-ex-2

#Lab 3 Question 5 (REVISED TO REMOVE EVERYTHING BUT THE ONES I WANTED (and uses starts_with()))

teacher_evals_clean <- teacher_evals |>
  rename(sex = 'gender') |> 
  mutate(teacher_id = as.character(teacher_id)) |> 
  filter(no_participants > 10) |> 
  select(-c(stud_grade_avg, stud_grade_avg_cur, stud_grade_std, stud_grade_std_cur, percent_failed, stud_grade_var_coef, stud_grade_var_coef_cur, class_duration, weekday, time_of_day, SET_score_1sem, maximum_score))
  select(-c(starts_with("stud"), percent_failed, class_duration, weekday, time_of_day, SET_score_1sem, maximum_score))

```

-   Character Example 1 (any context)

```{r}
#| label: wd-3-character

#Lab 5 Gym Investigation (edited as.Date to be as_date (awesome))

get_fit_now_member |>
  right_join(get_fit_now_check_in, join_by(id == membership_id)) |> 
  right_join(person, join_by(person_id == id, name == name)) |>
  right_join(drivers_license, join_by(license_id == id)) |>  #Joins
  mutate(check_in_date = make_date(year = str_sub(check_in_date, #Turn check_in_date into an actual date, not int
                                    start = 1,
                                    end = 4),
                                    month = str_sub(check_in_date,
                                    start = 5,
                                    end = 6),
                                    day = str_sub(check_in_date,
                                    start = 7,
                                    end = 8))) |> 
  filter(
    membership_status == "gold",
    str_starts(id, "48Z"),
    check_in_date == as_date("2018-01-09"),
    str_detect(as.character(plate_number), "H42W")) |> 
  select(person_id, name)

```

**WD-4: I can modify existing variables and create new variables in a dataframe for a *variety* of data types (e.g., numeric, integer, character, factor, date).**

-   Numeric Example 1

```{r}
#| label: wd-4-numeric-ex-1

#Challenge 3 Question 1

teacher_evals_compare <- teacher_evals |> 
  filter(question_no == 903) |> 
  mutate(SET_level = if_else(SET_score_avg >= 4, 
                             "excellent",
                             "standard"),
         sen_level = case_when(seniority <= 4 ~ "junior",
                               seniority >= 5 & seniority <= 8 ~ "senior",
                               seniority > 8 ~ "very senior")) |> 
  select(course_id, SET_level, sen_level)

```

-   Factor Example 1 (renaming levels)

```{r}
#| label: wd-4-factor-ex-1

#Lab 4 Question 4 (revised to have fct instead of as.Factor())

ca_childcare <- ca_childcare |> 
  mutate(county_name = str_remove(county_name, " County"),
        Region = fct_collapse(
    fct(county_name),
    "Superior" = superior_counties,
    "North Coast" = north_coast_counties,
    "San Francisco" = san_fran_counties,
    "North San Joaquin" = n_san_joaquin_counties,
    "Central Coast" = central_coast_counties,
    "South San Joaquin" = s_san_joaquin_counties,
    "Inland" = inland_counties,
    "Los Angeles" = la_county,
    "Orange" = orange_county,
    "San Diego Imperial" = san_diego_imperial_counties
  ))

```

-   Factor Example 2 (reordering levels)

```{r}
#| label: wd-4-factor-ex-2

#Lab 4 Question 7 (revised to have fct instead of as.Factor())

ca_childcare |> 
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(mc_infant, mc_toddler, mc_preschool),
    names_to = "age_group",
    values_to = "median_price"
  ) |> 
  mutate(
    age_group = fct(age_group, 
          levels = c("mc_infant", "mc_toddler", "mc_preschool")),
          Region = fct_reorder2(Region, study_year, median_price)) |> 
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x = study_year, y = median_price, color = Region)) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2008,2018,2)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(100,500,100),
                     limits = c(100, 500)) +
  facet_wrap(~ age_group,
      labeller = as_labeller(c(
      mc_infant = "Infant",
      mc_toddler = "Toddler",
      mc_preschool = "Preschool"
    ))) +
  labs(x = "Study Year",
       y = "",
       color = "California Region",
       title = "Weekly Median Price for Center-Based Childcare ($)") +
  scale_color_manual(values = colorRampPalette(brewer.pal(8, "Accent"))(10)) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(aspect.ratio = 1, 
        axis.text.x = element_text(size = 6),
        axis.text.y = element_text(size = 6),
        plot.title = element_text(size = 10),
        legend.title = element_text(size = 9),
        legend.text = element_text(size = 8),
        axis.title.x = element_text(size = 8))

```

**WD-5: I can use mutating joins to combine multiple dataframes.**

-   `left_join()` Example 1

```{r}
#| label: wd-5-left-ex-1

#Lab 5 Looking for the Hirer of the Hitman

person |> 
  left_join(drivers_license, join_by(license_id == id)) |> 
  left_join(income, by = "ssn") |> 
  left_join(facebook_event_checkin, join_by(id == person_id)) |> 
  filter(annual_income > median(annual_income, na.rm = TRUE),
         gender == "female",
         hair_color == "red",
         height >= 65,
         height <= 67,
         car_make == "Tesla",
         car_model == "Model S",
         event_name == "SQL Symphony Concert",
         str_detect(str_sub(date,
                            start = 5,
                            end = 6), pattern = "12")) |> 
  select(name, id)


```

**WD-6: I can use filtering joins to filter rows from a dataframe.**

-   `semi_join()`

```{r}
#| label: wd-6-semi

#Lab 5 Getting Interviews from Witnesses (Modified to nest a filter from person, then pulling transcript from interview)
witnesses <- person |>
  filter(
  (str_detect(name, pattern = "Annabel") & address_street_name == "Franklin Ave") |  (address_street_name == "Northwestern Dr" & address_number == max(address_number, na.rm = TRUE)))
           
interview |> 
  semi_join(witnesses,
  join_by(person_id == id)) |> 
  pull(transcript)

```

**WD-7: I can pivot dataframes from long to wide and visa versa**

-   `pivot_longer()`

```{r}
#| label: wd-7-long

#Challenge 4 Table of Means (revised to use fct() not factor())

ca_childcare_long <- ca_childcare |> 
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(mfcc_infant, mfcc_toddler, mfcc_preschool,
             mc_infant, mc_toddler, mc_preschool),
    names_to = c("type_care", "age_group"),
    names_sep = "_",
    values_to = "median_price") |> 
  mutate(
     type_care = case_when(
      type_care == "mfcc" ~ "Family",
      type_care == "mc" ~ "Center-based"),
    age_group = fct(age_group, levels = c("infant", "toddler", "preschool"))
  )
table <- ca_childcare_long |> 
  group_by(type_care, age_group) |> 
  summarise(
    mean_median_price = mean(median_price, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = 'drop'
  ) |> 
  kable()


```

-   `pivot_wider()`

```{r}
#| label: wd-7-wide

#Lab 4 Question 5

ca_childcare |> 
  filter(study_year %in% c("2008","2018")) |> 
  group_by(Region, study_year) |> 
  summarise(
    median_household_income_2018 = median(mhi_2018, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = 'drop'
  ) |> 
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = study_year,
    values_from = median_household_income_2018,
    names_prefix = "median_household_income_"
  ) |> 
  arrange(desc(median_household_income_2018)) 
  



```

**R-2: I can write well documented and tidy code.**

-   Example of **ggplot2** plotting

```{r}
#| label: r-2-1

#Lab 4 Question 7 (Revised to use fct not factor())

ca_childcare |> 
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(mc_infant, mc_toddler, mc_preschool),
    names_to = "age_group",
    values_to = "median_price"
  ) |> 
  mutate(
    age_group = fct(age_group, 
          levels = c("mc_infant", "mc_toddler", "mc_preschool")),
          Region = fct_reorder2(Region, study_year, median_price)) |> 
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x = study_year, y = median_price, color = Region)) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2008,2018,2)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(100,500,100),
                     limits = c(100, 500)) +
  facet_wrap(~ age_group,
      labeller = as_labeller(c(
      mc_infant = "Infant",
      mc_toddler = "Toddler",
      mc_preschool = "Preschool"
    ))) +
  labs(x = "Study Year",
       y = "",
       color = "California Region",
       title = "Weekly Median Price for Center-Based Childcare ($)") +
  scale_color_manual(values = colorRampPalette(brewer.pal(8, "Accent"))(10)) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(aspect.ratio = 1, 
        axis.text.x = element_text(size = 6),
        axis.text.y = element_text(size = 6),
        plot.title = element_text(size = 10),
        legend.title = element_text(size = 9),
        legend.text = element_text(size = 8),
        axis.title.x = element_text(size = 8))

```

```{r}
rescale_column <- function(df, vec){

    mutate(
      across(.cols = {{ vec }}, 
             .fns = ~ rescale_01(.x)
             )

}
```


-   Example (function stops)

```{r}
#| label: r-3-function-stops

#Lab 8 Question 1 (part of the code chunk)

rescale_01 <- function(vec){
  if (!is.numeric(vec)){
    return("Input is not numeric")
  }
  if (length(vec) <= 1){
    return("Input length must be greater than 1")
  }
  extrema <- range(vec, na.rm = TRUE)
  (vec - extrema[1]) / (extrema[2] - extrema[1])
}

```

```{r}
#| label: dvs-2-ex-4

#Lab 8 Plot Function

label_cleanup <- function(name){
  label <- rlang::as_label(enquo(name)) |> 
  str_replace_all("_", " ") |>
  str_to_title() |> 
  str_replace_all("Mm", "(mm)") |> 
  str_replace_all("G", "(g)")
}

plot_function <- function(df, xvar, yvar, colorvar){
  xlab <- label_cleanup({{xvar}})
  ylab <- label_cleanup({{yvar}})
  colorlab <- label_cleanup({{colorvar}})
  label <- rlang::englue("A scatterplot of {xlab} and {ylab}, colored by {colorlab}")
  sublab <- rlang::englue("With lines of best fit for each {colorlab}!")

  df |> 
    ggplot(mapping = aes(x = {{xvar}}, 
                         y = {{yvar}}, 
                         color = {{colorvar}})) +
    geom_point() +
    geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
    labs(x = xlab,
         y = ylab,
         color = colorlab,
         title = label,
         subtitle = sublab)
}
```

## Program Efficiency

**PE-1: I can write concise code which does not repeat itself.**

-   using a single function call with multiple inputs (rather than multiple function calls)

```{r}
#| label: pe-1-one-call

#Lab 5 Gym Investigation


get_fit_now_member |>
  right_join(get_fit_now_check_in, join_by(id == membership_id)) |> 
  right_join(person, join_by(person_id == id, name == name)) |>
  right_join(drivers_license, join_by(license_id == id)) |>  #Joins
  mutate(check_in_date = make_date(year = str_sub(check_in_date, #Turn check_in_date into an actual date, not int
                                    start = 1,
                                    end = 4),
                                    month = str_sub(check_in_date,
                                    start = 5,
                                    end = 6),
                                    day = str_sub(check_in_date,
                                    start = 7,
                                    end = 8))) |> 
  filter(
    membership_status == "gold",
    str_starts(id, "48Z"),
    check_in_date == as.Date("2018-01-09"),
    str_detect(as.character(plate_number), "H42W")) |> 
  select(person_id, name)

```

-   using `across()`

```{r}
#| label: pe-1-across

#Lab 7 Question 1

fish |> 
  summarise(
    has_na = sum(if_any(.cols = everything(), .fns = ~ is.na(.x))),
    across(.cols = everything(), .fns = ~ any(is.na(.x)), .names = "{.col}_NA")
    ) |> 
  select(has_na, where( ~ .x == TRUE))

```

**PE-2: I can write functions to reduce repetition in my code.**

-   Example 1: Function that operates on vectors

```{r}
#| label: pe-2-1

#Lab 8 Question 1

rescale_01 <- function(vec){
  if (!is.numeric(vec)){
    return("Input is not numeric")
  }
  if (length(vec) <= 1){
    return("Input length must be greater than 1")
  }
  extrema <- range(vec, na.rm = TRUE)
  (vec - extrema[1]) / (extrema[2] - extrema[1])
}


```

-   Example 2: Function that operates on data frames

```{r}
#| label: pe-2-2

#Lab 8 Question 3

plot_function <- function(df, xvar, yvar, colorvar){
  xlab <- label_cleanup({{xvar}})
  ylab <- label_cleanup({{yvar}})
  colorlab <- label_cleanup({{colorvar}})
  label <- rlang::englue("A scatterplot of {xlab} and {ylab}, colored by {colorlab}")
  sublab <- rlang::englue("With lines of best fit for each {colorlab}!")

  df |> 
    ggplot(mapping = aes(x = {{xvar}}, 
                         y = {{yvar}}, 
                         color = {{colorvar}})) +
    geom_point() +
    geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
    labs(x = xlab,
         y = ylab,
         color = colorlab,
         title = label,
         subtitle = sublab)
}

```

```{r}
  scale_color_manual(values = colorRampPalette(brewer.pal(8, "Accent"))(10)) +
```

## Data Simulation & Statisical Models

**DSSM-1: I can simulate data from a *variety* of probability models.**

-   Example 1

```{r}
#| label: dsm-1-1

#Lab 10 Question 8

mycifun <- function(beta0, beta1, n){
  
  if(!is.numeric(beta0) | !is.numeric(beta1) | !is.numeric(n)){
    stop("Make sure all inputs are numeric!")
  }
  
  intercept = beta0
  slope = beta1

  x <- runif(n, 0, 1)

  ep <- rnorm(n, 0, 1)
  
  y = intercept + x*slope + ep

  observed_data <- data.frame(x = x,
                            y = y)
  
  mod <- lm(y ~ x, data = observed_data)
  
  tidy_mod <- broom::tidy(mod,
            conf.int = TRUE,
            conf.level = 0.95)
  
  tidy_mod |> 
    filter(term == "x") |> 
    mutate(cover = case_when(beta1 >= conf.low & beta1 <= conf.high ~ "1",
                             beta1 < conf.low | beta1 > conf.high ~ "0")) |> 
    select(estimate, conf.low, conf.high, cover)
}

```

## Revising My Thinking

<!-- How did you revise your thinking throughout the course? How did you revise your thinking on the code examples you have provided in your portfolio? -->

\
Throughout the course, I have had the need to revise my thinking, with the most frequent offenders being saving an object, multiple function calls in one, and more recently, symptoms of lazy-itis on labeling my plots and being the most descriptive I can be. I also used a lot of superceded functions, namely factor(), and need to shake the urge to use those base functions that are named so nicely that I had used in other classes (before this formal R training).\
\
I feel like the overall theme of how I needed to revise my thinking was just to be more deliberate in what I was doing, and be conscious of which functions I am using and why I should be using those specifically.\
\
In terms of the portfolio, there were a couple situations where I needed to completely invent a new version of my solution (semi_join, anti_join), but otherwise, a lot of my revising was what I listed above. Stuff like superceded functions, and just other miscellaneous things I noticed as I was rereading my code. There were also a couple situations where a minor revision would change the way I solved a problem, but not in a big way (like selecting/removing based on logical values).

## Extending My Thinking

<!-- How did you extended your thinking throughout the course? How did you extend your thinking on the code examples you have provided in your portfolio? -->

I have extended my thinking best in plotting and visualizations. I find it hard to do so in things like dplyr pipelines, because there is generally a correct and quickest solution (apart from instances where I could've been more creative with semi or anti joins). But, it is interesting to move around, resize, and adjust titles, axes, legend titles, etc., and now that we have done tables, I have actually had the most fun messing around with all the extra gt package functions. I think that my tables and plots in this portfolio have shown that extension.
